cues.text: Chapter nine is an independent practice case.
You now apply what you have learned without a walkthrough from me.
I will set out the scenarios and the questions to ask of each, and the reasoning is yours to do.
The first scenario is fictional.
A transport app requires a driver to scan their face every time they log in.
Some users cannot authenticate in low light.
The system also retains the raw video indefinitely.
Start by naming the parties.
There are the drivers, who must submit their faces to work.
There is the company, which is responsible for fraud and for the safety of its service.
There are the passengers, who rely on the driver being who they claim to be.
Then there are the drivers who fail the scan, who bear the cost of its weaknesses.
The first task is to analyse the competing goals.
On one side is fraud prevention: making sure the person driving is the registered driver.
On the other are autonomy and equity.
Autonomy asks whether drivers have real control over how their bodies and images are used, or whether they must submit to keep their livelihood.
Equity asks whether the burden of failure falls unevenly.
A scan that fails in low light fails for particular people in particular conditions, and those people may lose access to work.
Neither goal is illegitimate.
Your job is to weigh them honestly and not wave one away.
Next, ask about actual necessity.
It is not enough that a face scan helps with fraud.
Ask whether it is genuinely needed, and whether a face scan at every single login is needed, as opposed to once at registration or on certain triggers.
Then examine the alternatives the exercise names.
The first is device credentials, where the driver is tied to a registered device and its own security.
The second is risk-based checks, where extra verification is triggered only when something looks unusual, such as a new device or an odd location.
The third is human review, where a person can verify identity when automated checks fail or are doubtful.
For each, ask whether it achieves the fraud-prevention aim with less intrusion on the driver.
Now consider sensitive-data conditions.
A face scan used to identify a person is biometric data.
Ask which special conditions apply to sensitive data in the framework you are working under, and whether the company can actually meet them.
Do not assume that ordinary permission is enough.
Then retention.
The system keeps raw video indefinitely.
Ask what purpose that serves once a login has been verified, how long retention is justified, and why raw video is kept rather than something less revealing.
Indefinite retention is hard to justify when the purpose has already been served.
Then accessibility.
Some users cannot authenticate in low light, so ask who is excluded and what the system offers them instead.
Finally, appeal.
If a driver is wrongly rejected, is there a clear route to challenge the outcome, reach a human, and be restored promptly?
From all this, your task is to recommend a tested, proportionate solution.
Proportionate means the intrusion matches the real risk.
Tested means you do not assume it works; you check it, including across different groups of users.
You must also state your uncertainties plainly, for example what you do not know about fraud levels or error rates.
You must define an owner, one accountable person or role responsible for the system and its outcomes.
And you must monitor subgroup failure rates, meaning you measure whether the system fails more often for some groups of drivers than others, and act when it does.
One more point: this exercise is independent of the live graded final.
It is practice, not part of your graded assessment.
The second scenario is this.
A product manager asks for analytics on private customer messages, to support optional advertising.
Work through five questions.
First, purpose compatibility.
Customers shared those messages to communicate with each other.
Is analysing them for advertising compatible with that original purpose, or is it a new and different purpose?
Second, lawful basis.
What legitimate ground, if any, supports this processing?
Remember that a lawful basis is not the same thing as consent, and you must be able to say which one is being relied on and why it holds.
Third, legitimate expectations.
What would a reasonable customer expect to happen to their private messages?
Most people would not expect their conversations to be read to target them with ads.
Fourth, access boundaries.
Who inside the organisation would see the content, under what controls, and how is access limited?
Fifth, less intrusive alternatives.
Could the advertising aim be met with aggregate analysis, which looks at patterns across many users and not at individual private messages?
Ask whether that gets the business most of what it needs with far less intrusion.
One caution is explicit in the source.
Do not assume that a broad terms-of-service agreement is meaningful permission.
A long document that users accept by clicking, without real understanding or choice, does not by itself show that they agreed to have private messages analysed.
Ask whether the permission is genuinely informed and specific.
Finally, the chapter closes with exam consolidation.
You should be able to distinguish seven pairs of ideas.
First, equality and equity.
Equality means treating everyone the same.
Equity means attending to differing needs and circumstances so that outcomes are fair, which is exactly the issue with the low-light scan.
Second, ethics and law.
Law is what is enforceable.
Ethics asks what we ought to do, which can go beyond or differ from what the law requires.
Third, consent and lawful basis.
Consent is one possible ground.
A lawful basis is the wider idea of a recognised justification, of which consent is only one kind.
Fourth, ownership and stewardship.
Ownership suggests control as of right.
Stewardship means caring for data responsibly on behalf of others, with duties attached.
Fifth, privacy and security.
Privacy concerns appropriate use and control of personal information.
Security concerns protecting it from unauthorised access.
You can have one without the other.
Sixth, innovation and responsibility.
New products create value, but the people who build them remain responsible for the harms and the fairness of what they release.
Seventh, individual and organisational accountability.
A person can be accountable for their own decisions, while the organisation is accountable for its systems, policies and culture.
Both matter, and neither replaces the other.
Use these seven distinctions as a checklist when you work through both scenarios and when you face exam questions.
